01From access to impact

FinMark Trust is an independent, non-profit trust established in 2002 to fight poverty and inequality in the Southern African Development Community (SADC) region by ensuring that underserved and vulnerable communities are included in the economy. Our purpose is to make financial markets work for people living in poverty by promoting financial inclusion and inclusive growth.

For more than two decades, our work has created a sustainable impact on the lives of low-income communities, achieved through partnerships with regional authorities, national governments, development partners and the private sector.

Our journey has taught us that access to financial services alone does not automatically translate into improved lives. FinMark Trust therefore pioneered an evolved approach to financial inclusion, developed with our peers in the Financial Sector Deepening (FSD) Network, that places financial inclusion within the larger development agenda and emphasises initiatives that deliver real economic impact: jobs, incomes, resilience and sustainable livelihoods. This shift from access to impact anticipated the global dialogue now taking place, including through the G20’s Global Partnership for Financial Inclusion (GPFI), to which FinMark Trust contributed actively as a key partner during South Africa’s 2025 G20 Presidency.

Our vision

An equitable world in which everyone is recognised and empowered to leverage inclusive financial markets to improve their lives and well-being, and to contribute to socioeconomic growth.

Our mission

FinMark Trust works tirelessly to address the challenges that affect the lives of people in poverty across the SADC region. We are convinced that financial inclusion is part of a broader development agenda that will ultimately improve livelihoods. While we continue to focus on the inclusive development of financial markets, our purpose and strategic focus now also emphasise initiatives that result in real economic impact.

02Our track record and impact

FinMark Trust has a strong track record of catalysing policy shifts, products and services that benefit people in poverty across the SADC region. Highlights of our impact include:

  • 43% → 22%2011 · 43%2025 · 22%Financial exclusion in SADC nearly halved between 2011 and 2025, while formal banking rose from 33% to 41% of adults
  • 4.7%>20%4.7%Average cost of sending USD55 across borders, down from more than 20% a decade ago — driven by reforms FinMark Trust helped catalyse
  • 15.6mFormal remittances processed in the South Africa–SADC corridors in 2024, achieving the 2027 target two years early
  • 35+Countries across Africa, Asia and the Caribbean covered by FinScope, the world’s most comprehensive demand-side survey of its kind
  • USD 1.4bnSettled monthly through the SADC RTGS system, whose development FinMark Trust supported since 2013
  • 15SADC central banks are submitting financial inclusion data to the regional M&E dashboards we support, with 100+ regulators trained

Further achievements that define our track record:

  1. Regional integration and policy influence.

    Long-term technical partnership with the SADC Secretariat and the Committee of Central Bank Governors (CCBG), including support for the SADC Strategy on Financial Inclusion and SMEs’ Access to Finance 2023–2028, approved by the SADC Council of Ministers, and national financial inclusion strategies in eight SADC member states.

  2. South Africa’s National Financial Inclusion Policy.

    As the World Bank-appointed coordinator for financial inclusion in South Africa, FinMark Trust supported the policy through to Cabinet approval and now supports the National Treasury in developing the National Financial Inclusion Strategy.

  3. SIBE Programme delivery.

    As lead consortium member of the EU-funded Support to Improving the Investment and Business Environment (SIBE) Programme, we delivered 71 assignments at a 91% completion rate over four years, strengthening investment frameworks, financial market integration, AML/CFT compliance and consumer protection across the region.

  4. Digital public infrastructure.

    Pioneering cross-border eKYC and digital identity work, including a strategic partnership with Co-Develop to support a federated eKYC ecosystem across all 16 SADC member states, aligned with the CCBG’s payment systems integration objectives.

  5. Livelihoods at scale.

    Through the Generating Better Livelihoods for Grant Recipients (GBL) project, thousands of social grant recipients have been profiled and supported into skills development, entrepreneurship and employment pathways. A national scale-up strategy for the project is now embedded in government systems.

03From evidence to action

Through our unique approach, we bring real change and benefits to people in the SADC region. As a market facilitator, we combine the evidence base to identify needs and blockages with the technical skills and partnerships to design, pilot and prove solutions in live markets — and then hand over to government and the private sector to roll out at scale, sustainably. Examples include our low-cost remittance corridors, digital financial identity and eKYC pilots, community digitalisation ecosystems, and risk-based AML/CFT approaches adopted by regulators and financial service providers.

We are passionate about Africa and are proudly a vehicle for African professionals who share our excitement about financial and economic inclusion in the SADC region. Our team reflects a diverse range of Africans with deep-rooted ambition and commitment to a financially inclusive region.

Deep local presence and reach built over more than 20 years, with country presence in South Africa, Botswana, Zimbabwe, Eswatini, Lesotho and Malawi, programme activity across the region, and ready access to stakeholders and policymakers, including at the SADC Secretariat.

04The SADC challenge: why access is not enough

Poverty remains one of the SADC regional economic community’s most significant challenges, with approximately half of the population living on less than USD1 a day, high youth unemployment, high levels of informality, food insecurity and acute vulnerability to climate change. The financial sector remains relatively underdeveloped, limiting access to finance, particularly for micro, small and medium enterprises (MSMEs), and constraining long-term, local-currency investment finance.

At the same time, financial inclusion in the region has improved markedly: financial exclusion fell from 43% of adults in 2011 to 22% in 2025. Yet FinScope data across several countries show that, despite gains in access, large segments of the population remain financially vulnerable. This disconnect between rising financial access and stagnant well-being is precisely what FinMark Trust aims to respond to. Our work moves beyond counting accounts to evaluating real improvements in financial health, resilience and ecosystem sustainability. We want inclusion to translate into jobs, incomes and improved livelihoods, especially for women, youth and the informal sector.

Our theory of change targets impact across three clusters: inclusive economic growth (incomes and jobs for low-income people); increased access to basic goods and services; and a stable, sustainable future characterised by resilience, equality and a green economy.

05Five priorities for real economic impact

Under our Strategic Framework 2024–2027, our programme work is organised around five strategic priorities, supported by four cross-cutting themes. We leverage regional and country stakeholders to catalyse and embed change, combining regional approaches and joint convening with implementation in Botswana, Eswatini, Lesotho, Malawi, South Africa and Zimbabwe.

BotswanaEswatiniLesothoMalawiSouth AfricaZimbabwe

i. Regional financial integration, trade and financial inclusion

We support SADC in achieving its regional financial integration and investment objectives under the Finance and Investment Protocol and the SADC Strategy on Financial Inclusion and SMEs’ Access to Finance 2023–2028. Our work spans cross-border remittances and payments, first-mile digitisation, digital financial identity and eKYC, formalisation of cross-border capital flows, informal cross-border trade, and financial inclusion coordination and measurement, including the SADC financial inclusion and remittances data portals and M&E dashboards. Our cross-border remittances work remains ground-breaking: costs on key corridors have fallen towards the G20 target, formal volumes continue to grow. We are also advancing regulatory reforms including a regional CDD/KYC process for remittance service providers to be linked to national ID systems to enable non-bank providers to offer low-risk digital wallets for undocumented migrants.

ii. Growth and resilience of smallholder farmers and MSMEs

Our supplier development programmes in Lesotho, Eswatini and Botswana support smallholder farmers and MSMEs with access to finance, access to markets, productivity improvements and national frameworks for supplier development. We also lead informal MSME support work: in partnership with the World Bank, the National Treasury and the Department of Small Business Development, we developed and are supporting the implementation of a policy framework for informal MSMEs in South Africa. Green finance, climate adaptation and green-economy opportunities, including community incomes through waste management and recycling, form a growing part of this portfolio.

iii. Local community empowerment through digitalisation

Our Inclusive Payments Digitalisation Programme (IPDP), funded by the Swiss State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO) and in partnership with the South African Reserve Bank, builds digital ecosystems in low-income communities. The community digitalisation pilots in Thembisa and Hammanskraal have onboarded 355 merchants to encourage the use of digital financial solutions for their businesses. They are supported by digital and financial literacy training and community liaison officers who are available to support the merchants and community with any blockages to digital financial services they encounter. Our digitalising incomes project protects informal and low-income workers, such as tip-dependent service workers, from being left behind in a digitised economy, with over 1,000 participants piloting digital tipping solutions.

1,000+over 1,000 participants piloting digital tipping solutions

iv. Better livelihoods for social protection grant recipients

The Generating Better Livelihoods for Grant Recipients (GBL) project is a flagship, government-led partnership with the DSD, SASSA, the National Development Agency and BRAC International, based on the globally proven BRAC graduation model. The project links Child Support Grant recipients, mostly young women, to employment, entrepreneurship and skills development pathways. The project is now being integrated into government delivery systems with a long-term national scale-up strategy, attracting regional interest for adaptation beyond South Africa.

v. Women and youth empowerment

Gender equality and women’s economic empowerment are mainstreamed across all our programmes, guided by our organisation-wide gender strategy and Gender Action Plan. We have integrated Women’s Economic Empowerment (WEE) indicators into FinScope surveys, strengthened gender-disaggregated data systems for SADC regulators and financial service providers. We also run targeted diagnostics and interventions for women cross-border traders, women remitters and vulnerable women workers, including in partnership with UN Women. Youth empowerment is prioritised through skills, entrepreneurship and employment linkages across our programmes.

06From data to decisions

FinMark Trust has always prioritised data and analytics, having pioneered the FinScope survey methodology in the early 2000s. FinScope Consumer and MSME surveys remain the gold standard in demand-side financial inclusion measurement. Conducted in more than 35 countries across Africa, Asia and the Caribbean, FinScope surveys inform policy decisions and industry conversations globally. Between full baseline surveys, the lighter-touch mobile FinScope Tracker allows countries to monitor key financial inclusion indicators on an ongoing basis, without the cost and lead time for a full survey cycle.

For more than two decades, FinScope has provided governments, regulators, development partners and the private sector with the evidence needed to design and monitor financial inclusion and economic development interventions. As the originator of the FinScope methodology, FinMark Trust has built one of the world's most extensive demand-side datasets on household and MSME financial behaviour, enabling trend analysis, policy formulation and market development across multiple regions.

Our data capabilities include supply- and demand-side data collection using multiple tools and methodologies (including mixed-mode and mobile approaches), advanced analytics, and the development of insights and evidence to drive impactful, targeted market initiatives. We measure financial health using a UNSGSA-aligned indicator, and we continue to deepen real economy-related measurement in areas such as informality, gender (WEE indicators), climate and green finance, and business resilience.

Our data portals, including the FinMark Trust data portal and the SADC financial inclusion and remittances portals we manage on behalf of the CCBG, help stakeholders make informed, data-driven decisions through accessible interfaces, with datasets available for direct download. We have also formalised a data training and capacity-building offering, spanning virtual and in-country training, field visits and support for regulators, national statistics offices, policymakers, FSD counterparts and financial service providers.

07Partnerships for impact

Our current and recent funding partners include the Swiss State Secretariat for Economic Affairs (SECO), the World Bank Group, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation, the Mastercard Foundation, BRAC International, FSD Africa, the South African Reserve Bank, UNCDF, UN Women, UK Aid (FCDO), the European Union (via SADC), the Alliance for Financial Inclusion (AFI), Access to Finance Rwanda, Co-Develop, and the Centre for Financial Inclusion.

We are a proud member of the FSD Network, a family of ten financial sector deepening organisations across Africa working to make financial markets work for the poor. In 2026, FinMark Trust also became a member of the Global Anti-Scam Alliance (GASA).

Governance and institutional strength

23consecutive unqualified audits

  • Financial integrity.

    FinMark Trust has achieved 23 consecutive unqualified audits, reflecting robust internal controls, compliance processes and prudent stewardship of donor resources. Our financial statements are independently audited in accordance with the IFRS for SMEs Accounting Standard and the requirements of the Trust Deed.

  • Sound governance.

    Governance processes are continuously strengthened through the review and implementation of updated policies and frameworks, supporting clear decision-making, accountability and alignment with strategic priorities.

  • Leadership continuity.

    A structured succession framework and ongoing leadership development strengthen our leadership pipeline and institutional resilience.

  • People and culture.

    Annual staff climate surveys reflect high levels of engagement, trust and organisational commitment, supported by a flexible, remote-enabled working environment and regular salary benchmarking.

  • Growing the next generation.

    Our internship programme bridges academic learning and the professional world; in 2025, three interns secured full-time or contractual roles within the organisation.
